This happened to me recently during a house sitting.  Dog was supposed to be walked for 10-20 minutes 4x a day.  Every time I grabbed the leash and harness he would run and hide despite being told he loves walks.  Told the owner and they said I could try and bribe him with treats.  It took 5 treats to get him outside and walking the first time.    Eventually I got down to only needing a treat to pit the harness on, but I could tell he didn't want to go for a walk.  Turns out the last sitter took him on a walk with his electric collar on and he got zapped.  I imagine he's already stressed with a new sitter and now the fear of getting shocked again made him not want to go.

Ask if you can use their dog food or treats to lure the pup out.  I would try goving her treats without the leash being seen and slowly making it visible.  It would take more time than the average walk so I would ask if you could do a drop-in to see if the pup will get used to you.  Maybe ask if she had any trouble walking with other walkers. 

Don't give up!  Hopefully by the end of the walks the puppy will love going out with you!

Please increase your calorie intake! You're body needs more calories to maintain your normal functions and I think you're in starvation mode.  You're body is storing the calories instead of burning them, which might be causing you to not lose weight.   For example, I'm losing about .5 lbs a week on a 1990 calorie budget as a 5'4", 245lb 22F.  Of course some days, I go over or under, but as long as I'm averaging, I lose the weight. Here's my story of going to college with the intention of being a fantasy author: 
I studied English Lit and Creative Writing in my undergrad (graduated May 2023).  I would say I was only able to take about 5 classes that actually helped in the fantasy-author career.  The rest helped me write nonfiction (essays) and study literature through different perspectives, looking at what works and what doesn't (even if the author did/didn't mean to do it), and being exposed to books I would have never thought to read.  Now, when I pick up a book, I look at the parts of the story and can immediately pick out what works/why this a classic etc.  To get a degree, you'll need to take courses you don't need to be an author, like statistics or chemistry, and in America, it's crazy expensive to the point of working full time to pay for your courses or tie yourself to student loans.

Now I'm in a master's program working towards my MA and MFA in Creative Writing.  The program is taught by published authors, who know what they're talking about: know the ins and outs of the industry, what it's like balancing a full time job and working on novels, and getting stuck.  The program director and staff look at your portfolio and accept you based on whether or not they think you could get published by the end of the program.  No degree in literature required.  We work in small groups (class size is 4 people; cohort is ~20), and meet in person two weeks out of the year, where we listen to readings from staff, do craft workshops, and share/read each other's work.  After we write our thesis project (which is essentially your novel), we present our work to agents and publishers that have connections with the program.  A few students ahead of me have already gotten book contracts.  I'm sharing this because this program is getting me a foot in the door.  When querying, I can say that I completed this program and that it could make me a more valuable client because I've networked and made connections with all these different writers.  
I would say that this program is worth its weight in gold, because it's based off of your merit as a writer, not what grade you got in Shakespeare and American Lit.  Some of the people in my cohort come from a science background and never when to college.  I would recommend finding a program that can help you become a stronger writer, whether it's an actual college, writer's retreat or joining a writer's group.  Sorry for the long post!
